title: How English spelling works
summary: Spelling is sound + pattern + meaning, not a random string of letters.
rule:
English spelling feels chaotic only if you expect it to be speech written down. It is really three systems working together:

  • Sound (phonology) - the sounds you hear, syllable by syllable.
  • Pattern (orthography) - the reliable ways letters combine, and the rules for adding endings.
  • Meaning (morphology) - words are built from meaningful parts that keep their spelling even when the sound changes.

Example: does is not spelled duz because it is simply do + es, exactly like go + es → goes. The pronunciation changes; the meaning-parts do not.

That is why this app never asks you to copy a word five times. Every word is practised by recalling it from memory (dictation), and every mistake is explained by the pattern or meaning-part behind it. Research shows this kind of retrieval practice beats copying, and that explicit, pattern-based teaching beats memorising unrelated lists.

examples.note: spelling keeps the meaning-part do, even though the sound changes
the g you can hear in signal explains the silent g in sign
a prefix + a base: just join them, no letters added or lost
the n belongs to govern, so it never disappears

title: Say it to spell it: hidden syllables
summary: Fast speech swallows syllables. Spelling keeps all of them.
rule:
In natural speech we squeeze many words: Feb-ry, Wens-day, diff-rent, lib-ry, prob-ly. If you spell what you hear in fast speech, you will drop letters.

Strategy: build a private “spelling pronunciation”. Say the word slowly, giving every syllable its vowel: Feb·ru·ar·y, Wed·nes·day, dif·fer·ent, en·vi·ron·ment, tem·per·a·ture. Then write one syllable at a time.

Meaning parts help too: different = differ + ent, interesting = interest + ing, environment = environ + ment, government = govern + ment.

In IELTS Listening the speaker may talk fast; your spelling must still contain every syllable.

examples.note: say en-vi-ron-ment; the n before -ment is in environ

exceptions: Some words are genuinely pronounced differently by different speakers (e.g. often). Spell the full form anyway.

title: Vowel letters: write every vowel, choose the right one
summary: For Arabic speakers the biggest risk is the vowel letters - especially in long words.
rule:
Arabic writing usually leaves short vowels out, so readers learn to rely on consonants. Research with Arabic-speaking learners of English shows the most common spelling errors are about vowel letters: choosing the wrong one (frant for front, defination for definition) and, in long words, leaving one out (orgnise for organise).

Two habits fix most of this:

  • Every syllable has a vowel letter. Count the syllables (or-gan-ise = 3) and check each one has its vowel.
  • Check the vowel with a relative. definition → define (you hear the i clearly); competition → compete; front, month, among, money use o for the “uh” sound.

Also learn the prefix pairs: de- (describe, despite, develop) vs di- (divide, direct, dilemma).

examples.note: the stressed i in define tells you the vowel
the e in compete shows the vowel

exceptions: The 'uh' sound /ʌ/ is spelled o in many common words (front, month, among, money, love) but u in others (public, number, budget). Learn these by word family.

title: Consonants: p/b, f/v and sounds with several spellings
summary: Arabic has no p or v sound, so p/b and f/v swaps are common. Some sounds also have several spellings.
rule:
p vs b and f vs v. Arabic has /b/ and /f/ but not /p/ or /v/, so learners often swap them (broblem, faforite). Say the pair aloud with your hand in front of your mouth: p has a puff of air and no voice; b is voiced. f is voiceless; v buzzes.

One sound, several spellings - chosen by word origin:

  • /k/ = ch in Greek words: character, technology, mechanism, scheme, chaos, stomach.
  • /f/ = ph in Greek words: physical, philosophy, phenomenon, emphasis, atmosphere.
  • /s/ = sc in Latin words: science, scene, discipline, fascinate, conscious, muscle.
  • /dʒ/ at the end of a word = -dge after a short vowel (bridge, knowledge, judge) and -ge otherwise (college, language, privilege).
  • /k/ at the end = -que in French words: technique, unique, antique.
exceptions: Some Greek-origin words are now spelled with f in American English (sulfur); British keeps ph (sulphur).

title: The no-change rule: consonant suffixes
summary: When the suffix starts with a consonant (-ment, -ness, -ly, -ful, -less), just join it.
rule:
A consonant suffix starts with a consonant: -ment, -ness, -ly, -ful, -less, -ship, -ty. With these, the base word usually does not change: just add the suffix.

  • develop + ment → development (no e after develop!)
  • final + ly → finally (the l of final + the l of -ly = ll)
  • open + ness → openness (n + n)
  • hope + ful → hopeful (the e stays before a consonant)
  • excite + ment → excitement

Two details: the suffix -ful has one l (careful, beautiful), and adjectives ending in -ic take -ally: basic → basically, automatic → automatically.

Many famous misspellings break this rule by adding or dropping letters: developement, finaly, accidently (accidental + ly → accidentally).

examples.note: e kept before a consonant suffix

exceptions: argue + ment = argument (e dropped)
true + ly = truly, due + ly = duly, whole + ly = wholly
judge + ment = judgement (UK) or judgment (both accepted)
public + ly = publicly (not publically)

title: The silent-e rule
summary: Drop the final silent e before a vowel suffix; keep it before a consonant suffix.
rule:
If a base ends in a silent e and the suffix starts with a vowel (-ing, -ed, -er, -able, -ous, -ive, -ion, -ity, -al, -ure), drop the e:

  • hope + ing → hoping   write + ing → writing
  • desire + able → desirable   fame + ous → famous
  • create + ive → creative   argue + ing → arguing

If the suffix starts with a consonant, keep the e: hope + ful → hopeful, excite + ment → excitement, complete + ly → completely.

Keep the e to keep a soft c or g before -able and -ous: notice + able → noticeable, manage + able → manageable, courage + ous → courageous. (Without the e, c and g would sound hard.)

Keep the e when the word ends in -ee, -oe, -ye: agree + ing → agreeing, see + ing → seeing.

examples.note: vowel suffix: drop the e (hopping is a different word!)
keep the e so the c stays soft
one t: writ-ing, the e is simply dropped

exceptions: argue + ment = argument; true + ly = truly; nine + th = ninth; awe + ful = awful
judgement (UK) / judgment (both accepted in IELTS)
likeable/likable, sizeable/sizable, useable/usable - both forms exist

title: The doubling rule
summary: One vowel + one consonant at the end of a stressed syllable: double the consonant before a vowel suffix.
rule:
Before a vowel suffix (-ing, -ed, -er, -est, -ence, -able), double the final consonant when the base ends in one short vowel + one consonant and that last syllable is stressed:

  • stop + ed → stopped, plan + ing → planning (one-syllable words: always stressed)
  • beGIN + ing → beginning, ocCUR + ed → occurred, comMIT + ee → committee

No doubling when the stress is on an earlier syllable: OFfer → offered, VISit → visited, TARget → targeted, deVELop → developed.

Watch the stress move: preFER → preferred, but PREFerence → preference (one r). Same with reFERred / REFerence.

British English doubles a final l after one vowel whatever the stress: travel → travelled, cancel → cancelled, model → modelling, label → labelled. (American: traveled - accepted in IELTS, but be consistent.)

Never double w, x or y: snowing, fixed, played.

examples.note: be-GIN: stressed, short vowel + n → double
OF-fer: stress on the first syllable → no doubling

exceptions: focus: focused (focussed also accepted in UK)
benefit: benefited (benefitted also used in UK)
parallel: paralleled (no doubling)
-c becomes -ck before e, i, y: panic → panicked, picnic → picnicking

title: The y to i rule
summary: Consonant + y: change y to i before any suffix, except one that starts with i.
rule:
If a base ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i before adding a suffix:

  • happy + ness → happiness, busy + ness → business
  • carry + ed → carried, study + es → studies, rely + able → reliable
  • beauty + ful → beautiful, vary + ous → various

Keep the y before a suffix that starts with i (otherwise you would get ii): study + ing → studying, apply + ing → applying.

Keep the y after a vowel: enjoy + ed → enjoyed, employ + er → employer, journey + s → journeys, survey + s → surveys.

This rule is very reliable - the few exceptions are worth memorising as a small group.

examples.note: y → i; say it slowly: bus-i-ness

exceptions: day + ly = daily; pay + ed = paid; say + ed = said; lay + ed = laid
one-syllable words often keep y with -ly/-ness: dryness, shyness, slyly

title: Prefix + base: keep every letter
summary: Adding a prefix never changes the base. When letters meet, you get a double.
rule:
A prefix is simply joined to the base word. Nothing is added; nothing is lost. So when the last letter of the prefix is the same as the first letter of the base, you get a double letter:

  • dis + satisfied → dissatisfied   but dis + appear → disappear (one s!)
  • mis + spell → misspell   un + necessary → unnecessary
  • im + mature → immature   ir + relevant → irrelevant   il + legal → illegal

The prefix in- (meaning not) changes to match the next sound: im- before b, m, p (impossible, immature, imbalance); il- before l (illegal, illogical); ir- before r (irregular, irrelevant). That is why these words have double letters.

Test: take the prefix off. If a whole word is left (appear, satisfied, necessary), write prefix + that word exactly.
exceptions: Some prefixed words are written with a hyphen in British English: co-operate/cooperate, re-enter (both accepted).

title: Hidden double consonants
summary: Many 'mystery' double letters are a Latin prefix that changed to match the next letter.
rule:
Latin prefixes such as ad- (to), com- (with), ob- (against), sub- (under) and in- changed their last letter to match the next consonant. The result is a double letter that you cannot hear:

  • ad + commodate → accommodate; ad + point → appoint; ad + tract → attract
  • com + mittee → committee; com + lect → collect; com + respond → correspond
  • ob + casion → occasion; ob + pose → oppose; sub + cess → success; sub + port → support

Strategy: if a word starts with ac-, ap-, at-, col-, com-, cor-, oc-, op-, suc-, sup- and the next letter is the same consonant, it is probably a hidden prefix + base. Also learn the famous “one-or-two” words by their parts: ne + cess + ary (one c, two s), re + commend (one c, two m), pro + fess + ion + al (one f, two s).

examples.note: re- is not doubled; commend has two m

exceptions: Not every word starting with a-, co-, o- doubles: across, among, apartment, omission (one m), cooperate.

title: -tion, -sion, -ssion, -cian
summary: The base word tells you which /ʃən/ ending to use.
rule:
Four spellings, one sound (/ʃən/ or /ʒən/). Look at the base word:

  • -tion - the most common; especially when the base ends in t or te: relate → relation, complete → completion, protect → protection, invent → invention.
  • -sion - when the base ends in d, de, se, nd or rt: decide → decision, divide → division, extend → extension, revise → revision, convert → conversion.
  • -ssion - when the base ends in ss, or in -mit or -cede/-ceed: discuss → discussion, express → expression, permit → permission, admit → admission, succeed → succession.
  • -cian - for people, when the base ends in -ic: music → musician, politics → politician, electric → electrician, technical → technician.

Watch for vowel changes in the base: pronounce → pronunciation, explain → explanation, repeat → repetition, describe → description, receive → reception.
exceptions: Some words have no modern base word: occasion, version, mission, passion, session, vision - learn them as whole words.

title: -able/-ible, -ance/-ence, -ant/-ent
summary: Use the base word and its relatives to choose the vowel in these endings.
rule:
-able or -ible?

  • If a whole word is left when you remove the ending, it is usually -able: acceptable, dependable, affordable, comfortable. If the base lost its e or y: value → valuable, rely → reliable.
  • If what is left is not a word, it is usually -ible: possible, visible, terrible, edible, feasible.
  • A related -ion word often signals -ible: division → divisible, permission → permissible, comprehension → comprehensible. A related -ation word signals -able: application → applicable, toleration → tolerable.

-ance/-ant or -ence/-ent?

  • A related -ation word → a: tolerate → tolerance, hesitate → hesitant, dominate → dominant.
  • Soft c or g (s, j sound) → e: innocence, adolescent, intelligent, emergency. Hard c or g → a: significant, elegant, arrogant.
  • After a stressed -er verb → e: refer → reference, prefer → preference, interfere → interference, differ → difference.
  • Verbs ending in -y, -ure, -ear → a: rely → reliance, endure → endurance, appear → appearance.

The rest are learned by family: exist → existence; maintain → maintenance (not maintainance).
exceptions: inevitable, capable, probable, vulnerable (-able after a non-word)
UK: dependant = a person who depends on you (noun); dependent = adjective
-ible after ss: accessible, permissible, admissible

title: -ise/-yse, -ous, -ary/-ery/-ory, -al/-le/-el
summary: British -ise and -yse, and the endings that hide their vowels.
rule:
-ise / -ize. British English usually writes -ise: organise, recognise, realise, emphasise. (-ize is also correct in British and is American; IELTS accepts both - just be consistent.) Some words are always -ise in both: advise, advertise, exercise, surprise, compromise, revise, supervise, televise, despise, comprise, otherwise. Some are always -ize: size, prize, capsize, seize.

-yse in British: analyse, paralyse, catalyse (American analyze). The nouns are the same everywhere: analysis, paralysis.

-ous / -ious / -eous: the i or e usually comes from the base: vary → various, courage → courageous (soft g), envy → envious. Many must be learned: obvious, serious, anxious, spontaneous, simultaneous.

-ary / -ery / -ory: -ory often belongs to an -ion family (prepare → preparation → preparatory; contradict → contradiction → contradictory). -ery often comes from an -er word or names a place/activity (deliver → delivery, bakery, surgery). -ary is the most common for adjectives (necessary, temporary, ordinary, voluntary).

-al / -le / -el: -al is usually a suffix on a base (natural, original, arrival, approval). -le is the most common noun ending (example, article, vehicle, principle). -el is rarer, often after m, n, r, s, v, w (channel, tunnel, travel, parcel, novel, label).

examples.note: keep e for the soft g

exceptions: stationary (not moving) vs stationery (paper, pens)
principal (main, head) vs principle (rule)

title: ie and ei - learned by family, not by rhyme
summary: The rhyme 'i before e except after c' is wrong too often. Use word families instead.
rule:
The old rhyme “i before e except after c” fails in dozens of common words (science, efficient, their, weight, foreign), so this app does not teach it. Instead:

  • The -ceive family comes from Latin capere (to take). Its members all keep cei: receive, receipt, deceive, deceit, perceive, conceive, conceit. Their nouns use -cept-: reception, deception, perception, conception. ceiling also has cei.
  • The /iː/ sound in other words is usually ie: believe, belief, achieve, chief, brief, field, piece, shield, grief, yield, priest, siege, relief.
  • The “ay” sound is ei: eight, weight, neighbour, reign, vein.
  • When c sounds like sh, it is cie: efficient, sufficient, ancient, species, conscience, deficient.
  • ie in two syllables is not a pair at all: sci-ence, so-ci-e-ty, va-ri-e-ty, qui-et, di-et, cli-ent.

A small group of ei words must be memorised: either, neither, foreign, sovereign, height, leisure, seize, weird, protein, their, heir.

examples.note: -ceipt also keeps cei (and a silent p)

exceptions: either, neither, foreign, sovereign, height, leisure, seize, weird, protein, their, heir - memorise
friend: ie with a short e sound - think fri-END

title: Silent letters - revealed by relatives
summary: Most silent letters are heard in a related word or explained by history.
rule:
A silent letter is rarely random. Very often you can hear it in a relative:

  • sign → signature, signal; design → designate; resign → resignation
  • muscle → muscular; autumn → autumnal; column → columnist; condemn → condemnation
  • bomb → bombard; crumb → crumble; debt → debit
  • government = govern + ment; environment = environ + ment (say the base!)
  • know → acknowledge, knowledge; exhaust - the h is from Latin haurire (to draw out)

Other silent letters come from the word's history: Wednesday = Woden's day; psychology, rhythm, character are Greek; island was respelled to look like isle. Knowing the story makes the letter memorable instead of arbitrary.

examples.note: the c is heard in muscular
p from Latin recepta; heard in reception

title: Unstressed vowels: find the stressed relative
summary: Vowels in weak syllables all sound like 'uh'. A relative where the vowel is stressed reveals the letter.
rule:
In unstressed syllables almost every vowel turns into the same weak sound, the schwa /ə/ (“uh”). So you cannot hear whether it is a, e, i or o: sep?rate, def?nite, gramm?r, comp?tition.

Strategy: find a relative in which that vowel is stressed and therefore clear:

  • definite ← define (de-FINE)   competition ← compete   repetition ← repeat
  • grammar ← grammatical   history ← historical   democracy ← democratic
  • comparison, comparative ← compare   preparation ← prepare   opposite ← oppose
  • legal ← legality   major ← majority   similar ← similarity

When no relative exists, use the meaning parts: se + par + ate (par = prepare, set apart), privi + lege (leg = law, as in legal).

examples.note: the i is clear in define
the a is stressed in grammatical

exceptions: Some schwa words have no helpful relative (e.g. calendar, cemetery) - for these the app gives a meaning or history note.

title: Homophones and confusables: meaning decides
summary: Same sound, different meaning, different spelling. Practised only inside sentences.
rule:
For these words the sound gives you no clue - the meaning decides the spelling. That is why this unit is always practised inside a sentence, as in IELTS Listening.

  • affect (verb: to influence) / effect (noun: a result)
  • principal (main; head of a school) / principle (a rule or belief)
  • stationary (not moving) / stationery (paper, pens - e for envelope)
  • complement (completes) / compliment (praise)
  • British noun/verb pairs: advice/advise, device/devise, practice/practise, licence/license - the noun has c, the verb has s.
  • lose (fail to keep) / loose (not tight); whether (if) / weather (rain, sun)
  • their (belonging to them) / there (place) / they're (they are)

Tip for the c/s pairs: the noun advice has ice in it (a noun); the verb advise ends like other verbs in -ise.

examples.note: Pollution has a bad effect on health.

exceptions: In American English practice and license are both noun and verb - accepted in IELTS, but stay consistent.

title: British vs American spelling - be consistent
summary: IELTS accepts both. Your target is British; the app accepts American but flags it.
rule:
IELTS accepts both British and American spelling. In Writing, examiners expect you to be consistent, so this app uses British as your target and flags American forms (still marked correct) to keep you consistent.

  • -our / -or: colour, favour, behaviour, neighbour, labour (US color...)
  • -re / -er: centre, theatre, metre, litre, fibre (US center...) - very common in IELTS Listening answers!
  • -ise / -ize, -yse / -yze: organise, analyse (US organize, analyze)
  • Double l: travelled, cancelled, modelling, jewellery, counsellor (US traveled...) - but British single l in fulfil, enrol, skilful, instalment
  • -ce / -se: defence, offence, licence (noun), pretence (US defense...)
  • -ogue / -og: catalogue, dialogue, analogue
  • ae, oe: paediatric, encyclopaedia, oestrogen
  • Single words: programme (TV; but computer program), cheque, tyre, grey, plough, aluminium, mum, storey, sceptical, moustache, pyjamas
exceptions: Oxford British spelling also uses -ize (organize) - accepted.
In computing, British English also writes program and disk.

title: Greek and Latin roots: word families
summary: Learn one root and you can spell a whole family of academic words. Greek roots also explain the strange letters: ph, y, ch, ps-.
rule:
Most academic (AWL) words are built from Latin and Greek roots. A root keeps its spelling across the whole family, so one root unlocks many words - this is the idea behind a word matrix.

Latin roots build most academic words:

  • struct (build): structure, construct, destruction, instruct, infrastructure
  • spect (look): inspect, perspective, spectator, respect, prospect
  • port (carry): transport, export, portable, report, support
  • dict (say): predict, dictionary, contradict, verdict
  • scrib / script (write): describe, description, manuscript, prescription, subscribe

Latin roots change inside a family. Many classic IELTS misspellings come from these changes:

  • maintain → maintenance, sustain → sustenance, retain → retention
  • pronounce → pronunciation - no o after the first n
  • permit → permission, decide → decision, include → inclusion
  • describe → description, assume → assumption, receive → reception
  • extend → extension, but intend → intention and attend → attention
  • a Latin root that is not an English word takes -ible: audible, visible, credible, tangible

Greek roots build the words of science, medicine, government and ideas:

  • graph (write), phon (sound), photo (light): paragraph, telephone, photograph
  • psych (mind), chron (time), bio (life), geo (earth) + -logy (study of): psychology, chronology, biology, geology
  • dem (people) + -cracy (rule) = democracy; tele (far) + scope (look) = telescope; phys (nature) + -ics = physics
  • prefixes: syn- / sym- (together), dia- (through), hypo- (under), anti- (against), a- / an- (not): synthesis, symbol, diagram, hypothesis, antibiotic, anonymous

The Greek spelling code. Once you know a word is Greek, its strange letters are predictable:

  • ph says /f/: phone, photo, graph, physics, philosophy, metaphor, catastrophe
  • y is the vowel inside the word: system, symbol, rhythm, typical, physical (/ɪ/); hydrogen, psychology, cycle (/aɪ/)
  • ch says /k/: chronic, technique, mechanism, character, chaos, school
  • silent first letters: psychology, pneumonia; rh: rhythm, rhetoric
  • British ae: archaeology, encyclopaedia, paediatric, haemoglobin, anaesthetic
  • -yse, never -ise: analyse, paralyse, catalyse - the y comes from Greek lysis

Greek plurals appear often in IELTS Writing: crisis → crises, analysis → analyses, hypothesis → hypotheses, criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena. The criteria are, not the criteria is.

One very reliable rule: the root meaning “go” is spelled -ceed in only three words: exceed, proceed, succeed. One word uses -sede: supersede. Everything else is -cede: precede, concede, recede, intercede.

examples.note: ten = hold: maintain → maintenance, ai becomes e
nunc = announce: pronounce loses its o
psych = mind, -logy = study of: silent p, y and ch are Greek spellings
sym- = together: Greek y, and syn- turns into sym- before b

exceptions: procedure has one e (proceed → procedure).
ph is two separate letters, not Greek ph, where two parts meet: shepherd (sheep + herd), uphill.
Not every Greek word uses y: crisis, critic and criteria have i.

title: IELTS Listening essentials
summary: Numbers, dates, plurals and the words that keep appearing in form-completion answers.
rule:
In IELTS Listening and Reading a misspelled answer scores zero, even if you understood everything. Capital letters do not matter, but every letter does - including a final -s.

  • Numbers: four → forty (no u!), nine → ninety, ninth (no e), eighth (one t, ends -hth), twelfth (keep the f), fifth.
  • Days and months: Wednesday, Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, February (Feb-ru-ary), August, September.
  • Plurals: if you hear an s, write it. Watch y → ies (facilities, activities) and irregular plurals (children, women, criteria, phenomena).
  • British -re words are frequent answers: centre, theatre, metre, kilometre, litre.

The other words in this unit come from typical form-completion topics: accommodation, travel, study, health, work, money and the environment.

examples.note: the u disappears in forty (fourteen keeps it)

exceptions: fourteen and four keep the u; only forty drops it.
